Reading machine learning papers

An interactive reading sample · 2026

Abstract. Explore equations, figures, tables, and text selection in this offline sample. It is not a published research paper.

1. Start with the question

A useful first pass identifies the problem, the proposed method, and the evidence. Separate the authors’ claims from the measurements that support them. Mark passages that depend on assumptions you want to revisit.

Select a few words in this paragraph. The reader offers Define, Relevance, Similar, and Ingest, keeping the passage connected to a paper conversation.

An input x i x_i and a prediction y ^ i \hat{y}_i are small parts of a larger argument. Seeing x i x_i again should preserve the same meaning while giving each occurrence its own reading anchor. The literal price $5 and the code $not_math$ are not equations.

2. Read the equations in context

Scaled dot-product attention turns compatibility scores between queries and keys into weights on values. Inspect each dimension before tracing how the expression fits into the model.

(1) Attention ( Q , K , V ) = softmax ( Q K T d k ) V \begin{equation}\label{eq:attention} \operatorname{Attention}(Q,K,V)=\operatorname{softmax}\!\left(\frac{QK^{\mathsf T}}{\sqrt{d_k}}\right)V \end{equation}

The normalization in Equation (1) matters because the scale of raw compatibility scores changes with the key dimension. A contextual explanation should connect the equation to its surrounding argument.

An aligned derivation makes intermediate assumptions visible:

(2) s i j = q i T k j d k , (3) a i j = exp ⁡ ( s i j ) ∑ r = 1 n exp ⁡ ( s i r ) , (4) o i = ∑ j = 1 n a i j v j . \begin{align} s_{ij} &= \frac{q_i^{\mathsf T}k_j}{\sqrt{d_k}},\\ a_{ij} &= \frac{\exp(s_{ij})}{\sum_{r=1}^{n}\exp(s_{ir})},\\ o_i &= \sum_{j=1}^{n} a_{ij}v_j. \end{align}

A small matrix is easier to inspect than a long list of coefficients:

A = [ 0.7 0.2 0.1 0.1 0.6 0.3 0.2 0.2 0.6 ] , ∑ j = 1 3 a i j = 1. A=\begin{bmatrix}0.7&0.2&0.1\\0.1&0.6&0.3\\0.2&0.2&0.6\end{bmatrix},\qquad \sum_{j=1}^{3}a_{ij}=1.

These numbers illustrate layout and row normalization; they are not measurements from a trained model.

3. Check the evaluation

Use tables to compare the conditions as well as the headline score. The example below is a layout fixture with illustrative labels, not experimental results.[1]

Condition Training data Compute held fixed? Uncertainty reported? Reading question
Baseline Same split Yes Multiple seeds Is the reference competitive?
Proposed method Same split Verify Check intervals Which change explains the gain?
Ablation Same split Verify Check variance Does the component matter?

Keep the objective next to the results rather than treating a single score as the whole story:

L ( θ ) = 1 N ∑ i = 1 N ( f θ ( x i ) − y i ) 2 + λ ‖ θ ‖ 2 2 . \mathcal L(\theta)=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}\bigl(f_\theta(x_i)-y_i\bigr)^2+\lambda\lVert\theta\rVert_2^2.

  1. Compare the same data split and measurement protocol.
  2. Check variation across runs, not only the best run.
  3. Read an ablation as evidence about a component, not proof of every claim.

4. Follow the references

Follow relevant source papers without losing your current reading position. Eligible shared conversions can be reused, while your conversations and personal annotations remain private.
